item.title: Version 0.33.12
item.description:
The character cue sits over its own column.
Two things looked wrong about a block of simultaneous dialogue — the names were not centred over the speeches, and the left column sat a line higher than the right — and both came from the same cause. The lines inside a block were being read as action.
What a line is gets decided from where it sits against the margins of the page: a name at the cue indent is a character cue, a line at the left margin is action. None of that holds inside a column. A name half way across the sheet is not at the cue indent, and a speech in the left column begins exactly where action begins, so the whole block read as action — which is why the names were not centred, and why one column carried the blank line that action gets and the other did not.
A block already knows. The row that made it a block is the cue, and what follows in that column is that person speaking.

item.title: Version 0.33.11
item.description:
Simultaneous dialogue, laid out properly this time.
The last release set two speakers in four columns, with the second name running one letter to a line. Each paragraph was being given a cell of its own instead of each speaker, so a character cue and the speech under it came out as two columns rather than two lines of one. A speaker is one column now, however much they say, and the cue is centred over it the way the page sets it.
A script already in a project still needs reading again to pick any of this up: Script ▸ Add Revisions… with the same file keeps the breakdown, the character descriptions, the casting and every settled finding on a scene that did not change.

item.title: Version 0.33.10
item.description:
Simultaneous dialogue is set side by side.
When two characters talk over one another a screenplay prints them in columns beside each other, and that is what the page means by it. Separating those columns so the right words belong to the right speaker was the last release; this one sets them the way they are printed. Three and four columns too — the width divides by however many speakers are on the row.
A script already in a project needs reading again to pick this up: the columns were flattened when it was imported, and a project keeps the script as it was parsed rather than the PDF it came from. Script ▸ Add Revisions… with the same file does it without losing anything — the breakdown, the character descriptions, the casting and every settled finding on an unchanged scene all survive, and only the scenes that really changed come back to be read again.
The pane also prints the blank line a screenplay puts between one element and the next, which it had been running together.
And quitting in the middle of a breakdown no longer crashes on the way out. The engine was being taken down by the process exiting while it still had work on the GPU; a quit now stops the run and waits for it to let go.

item.title: Version 0.33.9
item.description:
The revision marks, drawn properly.
One to a row. A speech set over four lines carries the mark four times, the way the page prints it, instead of once against the middle of the block.
At the size of the script. They were being drawn at the size the text view reports, which is not the size the script is set at — so they came out at roughly twice the surrounding text and clipped by their own box. Each mark now takes the font of the words it stands beside.
And they stay put while you scroll. Scrolling moves the pixels already drawn and repaints only the strip coming into view; anything drawn out in the margin, beside the text rather than in it, gets left behind. The marks vanished on the way past and came back only if you scrolled over the row again. The page repaints what comes into view now.

item.title: Version 0.33.8
item.description:
Three speakers at once, and four.
Simultaneous dialogue is not always two people. The columns are now counted off the page rather than assumed, so a row carrying three or four character cues side by side is read as three or four speeches.
Asking for a third column found a fault in the second. A character cue is centred over its column and the speech beneath it is wider, so the dialogue starts further left than the name above it — and a boundary drawn beside the cue cut through it. Two columns hid that; three merged two speakers into one line and said so at once. Each run of text now goes to the column whose middle it is nearest, which is what anybody reading the page does.
A revision mark is the one thing that does not follow that rule, and for a reason worth knowing: it is printed at the right margin of its own column, out in the gutter, which puts it nearer the next column's middle than its own. It goes to the last column that starts before it.
None of this reads a word of the script. A page is divided by where the words sit, so a production that marks every revised line and one that marks nothing are read the same way.

item.title: Version 0.33.7
item.description:
Two speakers side by side are two speeches.
A screenplay sets simultaneous dialogue in two columns, and the importer read every printed line straight across the page. The columns came out as one line: two character cues joined into a name nobody is called, and two people's words became one sentence belonging to one of them — which reached who is in the scene, what a quote says, and who reads it aloud. Each column is now read through on its own.
It is found by where the words sit, not by what is in them, so a script that marks nothing and a script that marks every revised line are handled the same way. Splitting the columns also puts each one's margin back in reach, which is why a revision mark kept turning up in the middle of the dialogue: it was at the right edge of the left column, in the gutter between the speakers.
This only applies to a script as it is imported. A script already in a project can have its margin marks repaired in place — Script ▸ Repair Margin Marks in Script — but two speakers already merged into one sentence cannot be separated after the fact, so a script with dual dialogue in it is worth importing again.
The reader no longer says the marks out loud. A mark with a number in it was being half-removed, so a voice reading a scene announced "seven" in the middle of somebody's line.
And the marks are drawn hard against the right edge of the script pane, at any window width, instead of being set as text where they could be selected and copied into a quote.

item.title: Version 0.33.6
item.description:
Margin marks belong in the margin.
A production that marks its revised lines or its alternates "*7" rather than a plain asterisk had those marks read as part of the script. They came out in the middle of the dialogue — fifty times in the first twenty pages of one feature, every one of them printed at the right margin where the page puts them. A mark is now asterisks and digits rather than asterisks alone, so the words read as they were typed and the mark prints out in the margin, the way the script prints it. That feature went from no scenes carrying revision marks to fifty-three.
Script ▸ Repair Margin Marks in Script does the same for a script already imported. A project keeps the script as it was parsed and not the PDF it came from, so nothing else could reach it short of importing again and breaking the whole thing down a second time. It fixes the quotes in the breakdown as well as the lines, since a quote with a mark in it stops matching its line and stops being highlighted. Nothing is re-read and no finding changes.
A line two characters say together is read by the first of them. "SCHMIDT/JENKO" and "SCHMIDT JENKO (CONT'D)" are one line with two names on it, nobody is cast under that name, and the reader fell through to the narrator — a line of dialogue read as description. It now reads in the first name's voice, and in the voice that character already has rather than a new one.

item.title: Version 0.33.5
item.description:
A rule that says no now says why, and you can tell it otherwise.
A comedy set in a maternity ward came back with "Delivery of baby", "Cutting cord", "Pulling out baby", "Spanking buttock" and "Shake ass" filed as stunts. None of them is one, and the filter that already refuses fist bumps missed every one — a list of phrasings only holds for the model that wrote it, and three of those are not contact between people at all. Shaking now counts as moving a part of the body however it is phrased, spanking goes with slapping where what matters is where it lands, and ordinary medical work has a short list of its own.
More useful than the filtering: a finding the rules turn down is no longer deleted. It arrives rejected, with its reason, in the drawer at the foot of the scene, and Put Back is next to it. A delivery staged across a gurney really is a stunt, and the rule should not be the last word on your scene. It also keeps something worth keeping when the rule is right — a scene with a cut cord in it wants scissors from props and a practical cord from effects, and how much of that you need depends on how much you see.
Stopping a breakdown and pressing Break Down again now asks whether to carry on or start over, instead of quietly starting the whole script again. Resuming reads only the scenes the run never reached; starting over reads everything under the model and rules chosen now.
Character descriptions and voice casting are saved. They never were: anything written in those fields was thrown away when the project closed.
And the last row of a list is no longer cut in half by the progress bar.

item.title: Version 0.33.4
item.description:
Stopping a breakdown and picking it up again.
Press Break Down after stopping part way and it used to start the whole script over. On a first pass that never showed, because the scenes already read are marked and the ones left are not. A re-run has no such mark — every scene was read the first time round — so a re-run stopped at scene 38 of 94 looked exactly like a finished script, and the app asked whether to do all 94 again, and did, from scene 1. A run now writes down what it still owes and takes scenes off as they land, so the button reads "Resume (56 left)" and carries on from where it stopped. It survives quitting, because the run people stop is the long one.
Character descriptions and voice casting are saved. They were being written to the project and never stored, so anyone who described a character or cast a voice for the table read lost it when the project closed, and the descriptions were quietly read off the page again on every open.
And the last row of a list is no longer cut in half. The bar that shows a run's progress was drawn across the bottom of the window rather than taking space of its own, so both lists ran underneath it. It reads as a list that will not scroll to its end, which is how it survived two attempts to fix the scrolling — there was nothing wrong with the scrolling.

item.title: Version 0.33.3
item.description:
The two scenes that cost you a quarter of the run.
A scene whose answer runs past the output limit is thrown away and read again in halves, which is three model calls for one scene. On a 94-scene feature two scenes did that and were 27% of a 45-minute run — and the densest of them overshot the limit by 119 tokens. The limit is now high enough that they are read in one pass: that scene takes 2m 39s instead of 6m 23s.
This was refused once, on the grounds that reading a scene in halves seemed to find more. Scored against a gold file over thirty scenes, it doesn't: recall is identical to the finding, 199 of 228 either way, while halving adds 59 elements that are not real ones and drops precision from 64% to 56%.
Scenes still split when one genuinely runs long, and the arcs are better when they do. A character in both halves used to keep only the first half's beat, so the arc column said "impressed" for a scene that leaves them dejected — the halves are now read in order and joined, with the intensity taken at its peak. Beats that said "Absent (not in scene)" no longer appear as rows for scenes the character is not in. And a synopsis cut off at the schema's length limit now stops at the last whole word instead of mid-word.

item.title: Version 0.33.2
item.description:
A scene's time is made of scenes.
The line under a finished run said "2.2 min a scene" on a breakdown that was taking 72 seconds. It was the whole wall clock divided by the scene count, and the summary is written after the second look — a different model, asked one question for every contested finding. Two different things were being added together and divided by the scenes. The per-scene figure is now made of scenes, the second look says its own name beside it, and the duration is still the clock in the room.
Measured on a 94-scene feature: scenes 1 to 5 took 99.9, 80.4, 24.4, 108.4 and 50.6 seconds, with the app itself costing nothing at all. A scene takes as long as the model has to say about it — one scene with 54 findings took six and a quarter minutes, while another of the same length with 19 took eighty-eight seconds.
The model also loads before the first scene now, rather than inside it, and the bar says so while it happens.
And a finished scene announces itself once instead of six times, which takes about ninety rebuilds of the whole script pane out of every run.

item.title: Version 0.33.1
item.description:
0.33.0 had the close-call rule backwards, and this corrects it.
A few hours ago it was changed on the strength of reading eight disagreements by hand and judging whether the second model's suggested category was right. That is the wrong question. Whether its answer is correct does not matter to somebody deciding what to read first; what matters is whether its objection points at a finding the run got wrong. Those come apart — by hand the model looked wrong most of the time, and against a gold file, where it objected the run was wrong half the time.
Measured by how often the run is actually wrong in each band: a confident disagreement, 100%; an unsure disagreement, 33%; agreeing without conviction, 8%; agreeing and sure, 6%. So every disagreement is worth reading, five to seventeen times the rate at which findings are wrong generally — including the unsure ones 0.33.0 dropped. And agreeing without conviction is worth nothing: it is the background rate, and it was nineteen of the twenty-seven things being flagged.
A close call is a disagreement now, and nothing else. On the sample that is eight things to look at rather than twenty-seven, and about half of them are real.

item.title: Version 0.33.0
item.description:
The close calls are worth reading now. The second model was sending you to the wrong findings, and this was measured rather than guessed: against a real breakdown with a gold file to check it, six of its eight disagreements were wrong — orderlies called cast when they are background, wet clothes called makeup when they are wardrobe, mud on legs called wardrobe when it is makeup, an ashtray called a vehicle.
The two it got right were its two most confident. Every wrong one sat below 0.8 confidence and both right ones at or above it, so a disagreement has to clear that bar to be flagged. Agreeing without conviction still counts: that is the model saying a finding is genuinely ambiguous, which is a different claim from thinking it is wrong, and it has nothing to be wrong about. A list of things to check first is only worth reading if what is on it is usually worth checking.
That pass also says what it is doing. On a feature it asks about a couple of thousand findings, which takes minutes, and it ran after the progress bar had gone — so the app looked finished and then sat there in silence, which is indistinguishable from the run itself having been slow.
All three panes scroll to the end. The last line of a scene used to sit half under the window edge where nothing could reach it, in the breakdown, the scene list and the script.
On speed, since it has been asked: a scene takes as long as the model has to say about it, not how long the scene is. Measured on one machine with one model, a sparse television scene produces about 290 words of findings and takes thirty seconds; a dense feature scene produces nearly 1,400 and takes eighty. Everything the app does around the model — saving, merging, redrawing — measures at zero. The rules added in 0.31 and 0.32 cost about 17% on top of that, which is the price of the model being told what a stunt is.

item.title: Version 0.32.2
item.description:
A butt slap and a forearm bump are not stunts either. The filter added in 0.32.1 was a list of exact phrases, which is right until somebody reports the next spelling of the same gesture: 'fist bump' was in it and 'forearm bump' was not. The gesture is now a part of the body and a word for touching it against somebody, so elbow, hip, chest, knuckle and shoulder arrive already covered.
A slap was harder. It is a stunt — choreographed, rehearsed, somebody can be hurt — right up until it lands on a backside, where it is a gesture. Where it lands decides it. A slap across the face is still a stunt, and so is a backhand.
Also worth saying, because it answers a question about speed rather than changing anything: a scene takes as long as the model has to say about it. A Perpetual Grace scene produces about 290 words of findings and takes thirty seconds; a dense feature scene produces nearly 1,400 and takes eighty. A 30-scene episode in twenty minutes and a 94-scene feature in two hours are the same engine doing five times the work on three times the scenes.

item.title: Version 0.32.1
item.description:
A breakdown is slow after a scene has been read aloud, and this is why: the speech model is 4.2 GB of graphics memory and it was held between reads so a second read would not cost a minute of loading. Nothing ever gave it back. A 27B engine wants about 21 GB, and when the two do not fit, nothing fails — the machine spills to system memory and every scene takes roughly twice as long, with nothing anywhere saying why. Measured on a 94-scene feature that is an hour becoming two.
The voice is released when a breakdown starts now. Reading a scene aloud afterwards costs a second or two to load it again rather than a minute, because the files are in the system's cache by then.
A fist bump is not a stunt, and neither is shaking your ass. The rule added in 0.31 says so in as many words and the model went on doing it anyway, which is what a prompt is — a request. This part is not a request any more: ordinary contact and dancing are dropped from stunts before a finding ever reaches you, the same way wardrobe that is only a character's name and lighting that only repeats the heading already were.
Written as phrases rather than words, because the words are the problem: 'fist' is in 'fist bump' and in burying one in somebody's stomach. And a dance on a moving car is still a stunt — a dangerous word anywhere in the line refuses the drop. That direction is deliberate. The cost of keeping one is a line you delete; the cost of dropping one is a coordinator nobody booked.

item.title: Version 0.32.0
item.description:
Break Down, pressed on a script that was already finished, did nothing at all and said nothing about why — while still writing a run into the history for a run that never started. It asks now, and then reads the whole script again. That matters more than it used to: the rules the model reads change between releases, and a rule about what counts as a stunt is worth nothing to a script that was read before it existed.
Your reviewing survives it. Anything you accepted or rejected keeps that answer when the model finds the same thing again, the pictures you pinned stay pinned, and something you corrected is not argued with by the next run. Findings are matched across runs by what they say rather than by an id, so a change of spelling between runs is still the same coat, and wardrobe for two people is still two entries.
A scene changes only when its own new breakdown arrives, so stopping half way leaves the rest of the script exactly as it was rather than hollowed out. And a run that comes back with nothing to say about a scene no longer erases what the last one said: no beats is not an instruction to forget the beats, and no synopsis is not an instruction to forget the synopsis.
What you say no to now goes in a drawer at the foot of the scene, folded away, with a Put Back on every line — rather than sitting struck through in the middle of the department it was wrong about, which made a scene somebody had been through read as more cluttered than one nobody had touched. Deletions are listed there too and say so: the item itself is gone, so the drawer tells you what it was rather than offering to undo what it cannot.

item.title: Version 0.31.0
item.description:
Intimacy is a department. There was no category for it at all — fifteen departments, one of them for animals, and nothing for the thing that has to be agreed with a performer before the day.
It reads the way stunts does: the question is whether the day needs an intimacy coordinator. Simulated sex, nudity whether or not the scene is sexual, sustained kissing, touching of a sexual nature, undressing, a scene played in a state of undress, simulated sexual violence — which is almost always a stunt as well and goes in both, because the choreography and the safety are two different conversations with two different people. Not a hug, a peck, a hand held: affection is not intimacy. It is the one department where the app deliberately over-reads, because a flag that was not needed costs a conversation and a missed one costs somebody finding out on the day what a scene asks of them. It prints beside stunts.
Stunts got stricter, in the other direction. The rule used to list moves — fight, punch, hit, fall — so a fist bump matched on the fist and a dance matched on being physical, and both arrived on a call sheet as stunts. It asks whether the day needs a coordinator now: contact is not violence, dancing is a choreographer, and a character described as tough is a description rather than an action. Still a stunt when it reads small: a slap, a shove, any fall that lands, anything a vehicle does beyond driving normally.
Both say whether a double is possible, because coverage decides it and the page says it: if the shot holds the performer's face, or the action runs straight on into the scene, there is no double and the day is planned differently.
Neither changes a breakdown you already have — they are what the model is told, so they take effect the next time a scene is run.

item.title: Version 0.30.1
item.description:
A character keeps one voice. 0.30.0 read a scene in a different person's voice every line, which is a bug with a cause worth saying: the model does not store a voice, it invents somebody who fits the description every time it is asked. Measured across six narrator lines that was a 94 Hz swing in pitch — a man, then a woman, then a man.
So the voice is minted once, from the description, into a short recording, and every line after that is spoken from the recording rather than from the words. One person for the whole scene, the same person tomorrow, and the same person in episode six.
What it costs: the intensity dots can no longer be spoken to the model as direction, because anything in this model that changes how a line is played also changes who is playing it. They are back to a few per cent of speed and pitch, which is weaker and cannot recast anybody.
Every row in the casting sheet has Another Voice, because a voice is minted once and a bad one would otherwise be permanent — ask for a barmaid in her forties and the model can hand you a child.
And a name is not a description. Characters the script never introduces used to be cast as 'The voice of Cole', which let the model pick anybody at all. They now get the least that is true of everybody — an adult, speaking, clear, not performing — and the sheet says plainly that the script never described them and this one is yours to write.

item.title: Version 0.30.0
item.description:
A scene can be read aloud in the voices the script describes. There is a voice model to download — about 4.5 GB, in the Models window — and with it a read stops sounding like a screen reader.
The casting is the script. A voice here is a sentence rather than a name off a list, and the script already writes that sentence, in the line of action where it introduces somebody. Maggie reads as 'MAGGIE REYES (40s), flannel shirt, sleeves rolled, a pencil tucked behind her ear' because that is what the page says. Casting for Reading Aloud shows what the script said about each person, with the scene it came from, and any of it can be rewritten. Describe the voice rather than naming an actor: the model has no idea who anybody is.
The intensity dots now do what they were always for. They used to nudge the speed and the pitch by a few per cent, which was the most that could be done with a system voice. Now the run's own few words go to the model as direction — 'frightened, hiding it' — graded by the number rather than replaced by it. The narrator is never performed.
Without the model, the Mac's own voices still read a scene, which is a different experience entirely.
Nothing leaves this Mac for any of it. The voice model is fetched by the same helper that fetches the breakdown models, pinned to one commit with every file checked against its SHA-256, and the speech is made here.

item.title: Version 0.29.3
item.description:
For anyone who has just downloaded the better voices: they join the compact ones rather than replacing them, so Ava ends up on the Mac three times — premium, enhanced and compact — and the picker was offering all three with nothing to tell them apart. Casting two characters from that list got you two people who sound identical, which is the one thing a table read exists to avoid.
One row per voice now, the best of each name, and the row says which one it is: 'Ava · American · Premium'.
The lists that match a voice to what the script says about somebody had fallen behind the same download. Isha, Matilda, Joelle, Noelle and Evan were not in them, so a script saying 'she' could still be cast against itself.

item.title: Version 0.29.2
item.description:
Where the better voices actually are. The app was telling people to look for a Manage Voices button on the Spoken Content pane, and there isn't one. The list is behind the small ⓘ beside System Voice, then behind the Voice row at the top of the sheet that opens — each voice has a download arrow, and the ones marked (Enhanced) or (Premium) are the ones worth having, about 40 MB each.
Six of this Mac's English voices are Siri's, and an app is not allowed to speak with them: cast somebody in one and their lines come out as silence. They are no longer offered.
The rest are now ordered by what they actually sound like rather than by what macOS calls them. Everything is 'compact' until you download better, which put the 1990s MacinTalk voices level with Samantha and Daniel. They are not level.

item.title: Version 0.29.1
item.description: The read button says what it is. The first question asked about the table read was where the button was: it was a speaker glyph at the end of a line of grey caption text, which is a reminder for somebody who already knows it is there. It says Read Aloud now, and Stop while it is reading, with Hold It beside it. There is a menu item as well, at ⌥⌘R.

item.title: Version 0.29.0
item.description:
A scene can be read aloud. Press the speaker beside a scene and it is read: a voice for each character, a narrator for the headings and the action, and the script following along as it goes. Casting for Reading Aloud, in the Script menu, is where you say who reads whom.
The casting follows what the script says. A screenplay usually says 'she' or 'he' in the sentence it introduces somebody in, and following that is the script talking rather than the app guessing. Where it says nothing, nothing is assumed, and anybody can be recast in a line.
The intensity dots shape how a line is said. The run already has a reading of how each character is playing a scene, 1 to 5, and reading every line flat throws it away — so it nudges the rate and the pitch, gently, and it can be switched off. The narrator is never performed.
Characters have a description now, taken from the line of action where the script introduces them — the script's own words, with the page they came from, rather than anything the app made up.
One thing worth knowing: macOS ships compact voices and downloads the good ones on request. The app cannot fetch them, because it has no network at all. If a read sounds like a train station, that is why, and the better voices are free in System Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Manage Voices.

item.title: Version 0.28.0
item.description:
A release that changes how the work is done now says so, once. The walkthrough is shown on a first run and then never again, which is right for a tour and wrong for a feature nobody knew to look for — the second opinion shipped two releases ago and the only account of it was a page every existing user had clicked past months earlier. So a release can declare itself, and anybody whose last tour predates it is shown those pages on the next launch. Not every release: a fix or a faster parser is not worth a window in front of what you were doing. What's New is in the Help menu too.
Buy the maker a beer is in the Help menu. It had only ever existed as the last page of the tour, so the one page that asks for anything was the one page nobody could find afterwards.

item.title: Version 0.27.0
item.description:
The walkthrough covers the part you do. It had eight pages explaining everything the machine does and not one saying how to review a breakdown, so there is now a page for it: what to add and change, why a hand entry survives a re-run and carries no mark on paper, and which findings to go to first.
It also catches up with the app. The download page says the second opinion comes down with the engine rather than leaving you to find it in the folder. The breakdown page says the model reads shots as well as things. There is a page for the one file meant to leave this Mac — the whole project, sealed with a password — and for pages that arrive labelled for an episode they don't belong to.
The second opinion can now be added on its own. It used to ride down with the engine and nothing else, so a Mac that already had a model had no way to get it short of re-fetching 16.5 GB. The Models window has a row for it, and the first launch after this update offers it once.

item.title: Version 0.26.0
item.description:
A second opinion on close calls. A small model now runs beside the breakdown model and marks the findings it reads differently, or agrees with but won't commit to. The scene list narrows to just those scenes, so a run that found a thousand things says which twenty to read first. It comes down with the engine on a new install; if you already have one, the app offers it once.
Props, set dressing, practical and visual. Use decides what something is, not who pays for it — a gurney a background orderly pushes is a prop, a couch somebody sits on is dressing. And an effect that could realistically be done for real is practical, not visual.
Camera and grip read off the page. A described shot suggests the gear it takes: a sweeping move reads as a crane, following feet as low-mode Steadicam, foreground and background both sharp as a split diopter. Rain on the page means a spray deflector on the lens and covers on the body.

item.title: Version 0.25.0
item.description:
A scene can be traced to the pages it arrived on.
**The pages travel with the scenes they carry.** Splicing a set of changed pages into a script used to keep the old script's page headers and throw the delivery's away, so a scene that came in from a revision could not afterwards be traced to the paper it arrived on. The header across the top of a page is the production saying what that piece of paper is — which episode, which revision, what colour stock — and it is the only thing that still answers "where did this scene come from" once everyone has forgotten how it got in.
Pages are now merged by their printed number: a reprinted 47 replaces the 47 that was there, a new 47A goes in between 47 and 48, and a page that arrived as an image with no text on it never replaces a readable one, because the words the script holds still came from the old page.
**So Move Scenes From Another Episode reads what is printed on a scene**, not only what an import was recorded as doing. That covers the case the records never could: an episode added as a script of its own leaves no import to read. Only headers that say "Ep" outright are believed — a show called Station 19 has digits in its name that are nobody's episode number.
**And when it finds nothing it says what it checked**, rather than a flat "nothing to move": the imports on record and what each one said it was, whether the pages name an episode at all, and that a scene which arrived some other way can still be moved by right-clicking it.
**A message no longer arrives under somebody else's name.** The heading and the text were set separately, so a heading left behind by whatever spoke last would sit over the next thing you were told — "Project exported" above "nothing to move".

item.title: Version 0.24.0
item.description:
Restart Now restarts.
A sheet stops an app terminating. Sparkle never quits the app itself — it sends a quit event and waits — and a quit event and an app quitting itself go through the same door, which an attached sheet holds shut. So Restart Now said "install", Sparkle asked the app to go away, the update dialogue was still on the window, and nothing happened, with nothing reported by either side because both believed it was still in progress. On Next Quit worked because that path takes its dialogue down first.
The dialogue now goes before the answer does, and so does anything else on a window: a reports panel or a half-read revision would have held an update up exactly as well.
This is the first release that can show it. The fix has to be in the version you are updating *from*, so 0.23.0 → 0.24.0 is the one where Restart Now closes the app and brings it straight back.

item.title: Version 0.23.0
item.description:
A project that can leave this Mac, and Restart Now that restarts.
**Export and import a project.** File ▸ Export Project (⇧⌘E) writes the whole thing to one file — scripts, breakdown, notes, marks, history and every picture pinned to a scene — sealed with a password. File ▸ Open Project File reads one back, on this Mac or another.
Everything else the app writes is sealed with a key that lives in this Mac's Keychain and is never anywhere else, which is the right answer for every file it writes until the project has to be somewhere else. So this one file carries the only secret that can travel with it. The password is stretched with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 over a random salt before it becomes a key; the contents are sealed with AES-GCM, so a wrong password and an edited file both fail loudly rather than opening with something else inside. Nothing about the project is outside the seal — not its title, not the names of its scripts, not how many scenes it has.
An import lands as a new project with a new key, never over one already here. Two Macs' copies of a project are two projects: they have been worked on separately since they parted.
**Restart Now works.** Sparkle does not quit the app — it sends a quit event and waits — and a window with a dialogue on it delays the quit. The dialogue now goes first and the answer follows it, which is why On Next Quit always worked and Restart Now never did.
**Scenes in the wrong episode can be put right in one go.** Script ▸ Move Scenes From Another Episode finds every scene that came in on another episode's pages — the label across every page header says which episode a delivery is, and the import keeps it — and moves them where they belong, with their breakdown, notes and marks.

item.title: Version 0.22.0
item.description:
A season in one pane, and four revision bugs a real episode found.
**The left-hand pane is the show.** Seasons, the episodes in each, and the scenes inside those — every level folds. A whole season sits in it and closes down to four lines. Click a scene in a folded episode and it opens there. Episodes are named the way a production names them: EP109, in the sidebar, in the reports picker and in the wrong-episode warning.
**Search whatever you clicked.** An episode searches that episode, a season searches the season, the show searches everything. The field says what it is about before you type, the episodes that have matches open, and following a result does not narrow the question.
**Revisions.** A whole episode of real deliveries — four revisions, each sent both as changed pages and as a collated script — found four things wrong, and each fix is checked against what the production itself sent:
- Pages that do not adjoin are no longer glued together. A delivery of changed pages is a few runs out of the middle of a script, and read straight through the first page of the next run joined the last scene of the one before it. One scene came out nine pages long holding another scene's words. - A scene ending at the foot of a run is a fragment even when the page does not fill. Five scenes in a single delivery were being spliced in at a third of their length. - A scene cut by a revision now leaves. A production cuts by printing the number against OMITTED, in the margin, where nothing was reading. - Inserted scenes read forwards: A1, B1, C1, 1 — not backwards.
Splicing each set of pages onto the draft before it now lands on that revision's own collated script with the same scenes in the same order.
**Move a scene to the episode it belongs to.** Right-click it, or Script ▸ Move Scenes From Another Episode to move every scene that came in on another episode's pages at once. The scene takes its breakdown, beats, notes and marks with it, and both scripts are renumbered around it.
**What a shot asks for.** A sweeping shot over a wide space is a crane; staying with someone's feet is a Steadicam in low mode; a foreground and a background both held sharp is a split diopter. The breakdown names the rig behind a described move.
**The script pane stops arguing with the hand on it.** Reading down past a scene break no longer drags you back to the top of the scene.
**Buttons that say what they do**: Import Episode and Add Revisions, named rather than drawn.

item.title: Version 0.21.0
item.description:
A revision knows which episode it belongs to.
Every page of a delivery carries a label — EP 110 - "A Sheriff...Sheriff..." - YELLOW Revision - 03/10/19 — and the episode is written in it. The import reads that label, and the file name behind it, and compares it with the script it is about to be spliced into. When they disagree it says so before anything happens, in the terms a production uses: these pages are 1x10, this script is 1x08.
If that episode is in the project, it offers to import into that one instead. A season lives in one project, so the right script is usually a few rows up in the sidebar.
This is worth stopping for because nothing fails when it goes wrong. The scene numbers simply do not match, so the pages arrive as new scenes, and what you get is one script holding two episodes — which is exactly how this was found: sixteen scenes of one episode sitting at the top of another.

item.title: Version 0.20.0
item.description:
A season in one project, reports that span it, and the scene order put right.
The scripts in a project are arranged as show, season, episode. Television numbers episodes in one run — Ep104 is season 1 episode 4, 208 is season 2 episode 8 — so the season and the episode are already in the name the production sent, and they are read out of it rather than asked for again. Seasons fold away, episodes sit in episode order with their number beside the file name, and a script whose name says nothing is left alone, because a feature is not season 9 of anything.
Reports cover the episodes you choose: this one, the whole season, or a few of them. Each episode is built as it always was and the sections put together afterwards, so every one opens with its own heading — which is what tells you whose scene 12 you are looking at.
Fixed: the scene list came back in two runs, with low-numbered scenes stranded behind the end of the episode. Splicing a revision places each arriving scene after the last scene below it, and when there is nothing below it the answer is the top, not the bottom. Scene 1 arriving into a delivery that starts at 13 went behind scene 84.
Fixed: Restart Now did nothing. Sparkle stages the new version and cannot swap the bundle while the old one is running, so it hands that back and waits — and the method it waits on was empty. Anyone on 0.19.0 will need to install this one by hand; from here on the button works.
Fixed: the script jumped under the hand scrolling it. Scrolling selects the scene at the top of the window, and every change to the selection was rebuilding the entire script — a hundred scenes laid out and compared — on the main thread.
Fixed: Import Revision never opened its file panel, from the button, the menu or ⇧⌘R. Two file importers were chained on the same view, and SwiftUI presents one and silently ignores the other.
Also: a project opens on double-click. The colour of paper a scene was printed on now reads as a band across the head of the scene and a heavier bar down its edge, in the script and the scene list both, rather than a one-pixel rule nobody could find.

item.title: Version 0.19.0
item.description:
Settings, a script you can mark by hand, and two departments that should always have been there.
Settings is at ⌘, and holds the size of all three columns. The script is in points, because a screenplay is set in one face at one size and that is the number you mean. The scene list and the breakdown are in steps, because they are ordinary interface text with no single size to name. Day, Night, or whatever the system is doing — the app followed the system, and the system is dark, so it was a night app whether or not that suited the room.
The script can be marked by hand. Select any phrase, right-click, and either file it under a department or mark it. Filing it makes a finding like any other, with the words kept as its quote, so the script marks them in that department's colour and the breakdown lists it beside the model's own. A mark belongs to nobody: it is for the thing you want to come back to and cannot yet name, and it says "look here" without telling everyone else the words are a props item. Both survive a re-run, as a note does.
Doing that meant rebuilding the script pane on AppKit. A selection cannot cross two labels, and SwiftUI gives the reader a selection and the program no way to read it — there is no version of "select the tea kettle and file it under props" that could be built on what was there.
Sound and music are departments. They were left out on the grounds that they are cut after the shoot, which does not survive contact with a schedule: a jukebox has to be cleared and played on set, a radio the actors react to is playback somebody rigs, and a song named in the action is a licence bought before the day. The prompt used to say in as many words that sounds are never listed. It no longer does.
The colours follow the convention every marked-up script uses — cast green, props red, costume blue, set dressing magenta, extras cyan, stunts orange, sound yellow, music light green. Six of them were somewhere else: cast was red, which is props, and props were purple, which is set dressing. On paper that is not a different palette, it is a wrong one.
Fixed: Import Revision never opened its panel — not under automation, on any machine. Two file importers were chained on the same view and SwiftUI presents one and silently ignores the other, so the button, the menu item and ⇧⌘R all did nothing and nothing reported a problem.
Fixed: the second character's line on the Character Arc chart doubled back across the page. Scene numbers are text, so the axis is a list of categories, and left to work the order out Charts took it from the order the marks arrived in — the first character's scenes set the axis and the second character's own scenes were appended after the end of it.
Fixed: the splash stood for four seconds and then the window did not come forward at all, which is a poor first impression for the one moment the splash exists to make. It is 1.5 seconds now, 60 per cent larger, and the window crossfades in behind it.
Fixed: listing the models folder happened on the main thread, so the permission prompt that folder raises froze the entire app for as long as it stood — including the splash's own timer and the failsafe meant to rescue it.

item.title: Version 0.18.0
item.description:
What is between two characters, a window you can rearrange, and a splash that behaves.
Character Arc gained a second view. Pick exactly two characters and 'Between them' reads the relationship itself rather than showing you two arcs side by side — those are different questions, and 'she is frightened, he is calm' says nothing about whether they trust each other. A short extra pass covers only the scenes they share and asks one question of each: where these two stand, on a scale that runs from at war through neutral to inseparable, who has the upper hand, and what shifts. The scenes where it changes are marked, found by comparing each scene with the one before it in story order. A couple of minutes for a pair, and it is kept, so it only happens once.
A new version now says so in a window in front of the app rather than a thin strip along the top that nobody reads.
Any of the three columns — scenes, breakdown, script — can be put away, from the View menu at ⌃⌘1, ⌃⌘2 and ⌃⌘3. What you leave showing is remembered.
The splash has no white card. The artwork floats with a glow of its own, and it opens over the middle of the window it is standing in front of rather than the middle of the screen. The main window now waits behind it instead of arriving at the same moment.
Fixed: a saved relationship reading stored scene numbers by position, so a revision that cut a scene would have quietly turned a reading of three scenes into a reading of three different ones. Readings now follow their scenes through a revision, and say so when the script has changed under them.

item.title: Version 0.17.0
item.description:
A sample you can open straight away, corrections that stick, and the arc opened up.
A script that is already broken down now ships with the app — 30 scenes, 349 things found, every department. The script is a synthetic benchmark and the breakdown is a real saved run of it, mistakes and all, because a sample where everything is right shows you nothing about what the reviewing is for. Three scenes are taken the rest of the way and the other twenty-seven are left as the model left them. It is on the start screen next to New Project, and you can delete it like any other project.
Corrections now teach the next run. Moving something between departments, renaming it, or deleting it are three different lessons, and all three used to be thrown away. They are kept on the project — a season — so episode one teaches it the show's vocabulary and the rest get it for free. Changing something asks one skippable question about why, since the model being wrong and your production calling it something else look identical from outside. Changes (⇧⌘Y) has a second tab listing what it has learned, with a Forget beside each one. None of it leaves this Mac; the app has no way to send it anywhere.
Character Arc: the columns are yours now. It opens as a DP's view, but any department the breakdown found can be a column, and 'Only theirs' narrows them to things that name the character — so the same scenes become a costume continuity list. Up to four characters can go on it at once, each with a line on the chart and a column in the table, so the scene where one goes quiet and the other doesn't is a row you can point at. The CSV exports what is on screen.
Also: scene numbers in the rolling script are three times the size and sit under the rule, so you can find one going past. And the intensity dots now say what they are counting — 1 calm to 5 extreme, the model's reading of how hard a character is playing the scene.

item.title: Version 0.16.0
item.description:
Six things, mostly about the window.
The model picker and the Break Down button had been pushed off the toolbar into an overflow chevron. They now have the trailing edge to themselves, everything else moved to the leading side, and the windows that were unlabelled icons are in a new Script menu with a shortcut each. The default window is wide enough to show all of it.
The script pane shows the whole script in one scroll, with a marked line at each scene carrying its number, its eighths and the colour of paper it was printed on. Scroll past a marker and the breakdown follows you; pick a scene and the script scrolls to it.
There is a switch for each department above the breakdown, so you can walk a whole episode looking at nothing but the props.
A run now says what it found when it finishes — the counts, the departments, how long it took, and the parts worth a second look: scenes it found nothing in and quotes it could not trace back to the page.
Reports and prints carry a watermark, on by default. The name is read off the script you imported: distribution services stamp the recipient into the copy, and paperwork printed from that copy should say which copy it came from. You can change it or switch it off.

item.title: Version 0.15.1
item.description: The walkthrough's last page shows a code to point a phone at rather than a link.

item.title: Version 0.15.0
item.description: A board for everything pinned in a script, and pictures of one particular thing rather than a whole scene. Crash reports are written locally when something goes wrong — never sent anywhere, and they hold no part of any script.

item.title: Version 0.14.0
item.description: Finish a breakdown by hand: add what the model missed, correct what it found, write notes on scenes. Everything you change is recorded and survives a re-run. Pin reference pictures to a scene and print them as a look book — location and camera details are taken out of every image on the way in.

item.title: Version 0.13.0
item.description: Edit a breakdown by hand: add what the model missed, correct what it found, write notes on scenes. Everything you change is recorded and survives a re-run. Importing a revision now asks what should happen to notes on the scenes it changes.

item.title: Version 0.12.0
item.description: A walkthrough on first run and from the Help menu. Updates now say that the app has to restart to finish installing, and let you choose when.

item.title: Version 0.11.1
item.description: Fixes the launch check, which found updates and then reported none.
